title: Linear Equations in One Variable
summary: A linear equation says two expressions are equal, and somewhere inside is an unknown we call a variable (usually x). Solving means finding the single value of x that makes the statement true. We do it by keeping the equation balanced: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other.

concept_sections.heading: An equation is a balance
concept_sections.explanation: Think of '=' as the center of a scale. The left side and the right side weigh the same. In 'x + 3 = 7', the left side is 'x + 3' and the right side is '7'. Our job is to figure out what x has to be so both sides truly balance. Here, x = 4, because 4 + 3 = 7. At this level you can often just ask: 'what number plus 3 gives 7?'

concept_sections.heading: Undo operations to isolate x
concept_sections.explanation: Instead of guessing, we isolate x by undoing whatever is attached to it. Addition is undone by subtraction, and multiplication is undone by division. For 'x + 3 = 7', subtract 3 from BOTH sides: x + 3 - 3 = 7 - 3, which gives x = 4. The golden rule: whatever you do to one side, do to the other, so the balance is never broken.

concept_sections.heading: Two-step equations
concept_sections.explanation: Many equations attach two things to x, like '2x + 1 = 9'. Undo them in reverse order of operations: first undo the addition, then the multiplication. Subtract 1 from both sides to get 2x = 8, then divide both sides by 2 to get x = 4. The pattern is always: peel away the outer operation first, working your way in toward x.

concept_sections.heading: Variables on both sides and distribution
concept_sections.explanation: Sometimes x appears on both sides, or is wrapped in parentheses, like '3(x - 2) = x + 4'. First distribute: 3x - 6 = x + 4. Then gather the x-terms on one side by subtracting x from both: 2x - 6 = 4. Then solve the two-step equation: add 6 to get 2x = 10, divide by 2 to get x = 5. The strategy is: simplify each side, collect variables on one side and numbers on the other, then isolate.

concept_sections.heading: Special cases: no solution and all solutions
concept_sections.explanation: Not every linear equation has exactly one answer. If solving leads to a false statement like '5 = 8', there is NO solution — the two sides can never balance (e.g. 2x + 3 = 2x + 6). If it leads to an always-true statement like '4 = 4', then EVERY number works — it is an identity (e.g. 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2). Recognizing these tells you the variable has cancelled out, which is a feature, not a mistake.

real_world_examples.title: Splitting a restaurant bill
real_world_examples.scenario: You and 3 friends (4 people total) share a meal. The total bill is $52, which already includes a flat $8 delivery fee. You want to know what the food cost per person was before the fee.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Let x be the food cost per person. The equation is 4x + 8 = 52. Subtract 8 to get 4x = 44, then divide by 4 to get x = 11. Each person's food was $11. This is exactly a two-step linear equation.

real_world_examples.title: Phone plan break-even
real_world_examples.scenario: Plan A charges a $20 monthly fee plus $0.10 per GB. Plan B charges a flat $35. You want to know how many GB make the two plans cost the same.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Let x be gigabytes. Set the costs equal: 20 + 0.10x = 35. Subtract 20 to get 0.10x = 15, divide by 0.10 to get x = 150 GB. Below 150 GB Plan A is cheaper; above it, Plan B wins. This is a variables-in-context linear equation.

real_world_examples.title: Filling a road-trip gas tank
real_world_examples.scenario: Your tank already has 3 gallons. The pump adds 2 gallons every minute. Your tank holds 15 gallons. You want to know how long until it's full.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Let x be minutes pumping. The equation is 3 + 2x = 15. Subtract 3 to get 2x = 12, divide by 2 to get x = 6 minutes. The starting amount is the constant and the pump rate is the coefficient of x.
